_metadata.method: partner arm: pool UniProt curated interaction partners of known autoantigens (epitope-spreading prior); filter hubs (specificity>=min) and thin annotation (degree>=min); rank by support (# known antigens linked), then specificity, then the nuclear/NA prior. specificity = links-to-known-antigens / total partners.
_metadata.framing: Candidates are CITED HYPOTHESES for expert review, not confirmed discoveries.
_metadata.caveat: Partner arm finds complex-members well; standalone antigens (e.g. Ro60, no curated interactions) are invisible to it — a known coverage gap. Specificity controls for hub bias (e.g. HTT, 860 partners, correctly demoted).

ranking.order: support, then specificity, then nuclear/NA prior
ranking.note: Transparent multi-signal ranking; filters/order are a documented first pass.

## Assessment: SF3A2 (Q15428) as a potential SLE autoantigen

**What the protein is**
- SF3A2 (Splicing factor 3A subunit 2, "SAP62") is a component of the **17S U2 snRNP** spliceosome complex, specifically part of the **SF3A subcomplex** (SF3A1/SF3A2/SF3A3). It helps assemble the U2 snRNP and recognizes the intron branch site during pre-mRNA splicing. [UniProt Q15428](https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q15428/entry)
- Note on classification: although SF3A2 physically associates with Sm proteins (Sm-B/B', Sm-D1/2/3) and U1-C, its own home is the **U2 snRNP / SF3A subcomplex**. This is *not* one of the named, clinically tested SLE autoantigen particles (anti-Sm, anti-U1-RNP, anti-Ro/La, etc.). Physical association with Sm antigens is interaction, not membership in a recognized autoantigen complex — so complex-level autoantigen status does not automatically transfer to SF3A2.

**Structural confidence (context only, not autoantigen evidence)**
- AlphaFold mean pLDDT = 64.1/100 ("Low" confidence) — the predicted 3D model is of limited reliability, likely reflecting intrinsically disordered regions. [AlphaFold Q15428](https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q15428)

**Literature search for autoantigen evidence** — I ran five queries:
- "SF3A2 autoantibody autoantigen lupus" → no papers found.
- "SF3A2 SAP62 autoantibody autoimmune" → one off-topic COVID-vaccine myocarditis case report, nothing on SF3A2 as an autoantigen. [MED/34133883](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/34133883)
- "SF3a splicing factor autoantibody autoimmune disease" → the only relevant hit concerned a **different protein**, anti-**SF3B1** (a SF3B-subcomplex protein) as a marker in hepatocellular carcinoma — not SF3A2 and not SLE. [MED/29954402](https://europepmc.org/article/MED/29954402)
- "splicing factor 3A subunit autoantibody SLE" and "U2 snRNP SF3A autoantigen connective tissue disease" → only generic SLE/autoimmunity reviews and an unrelated 1993 meeting abstract; nothing linking SF3A2 to autoantibodies.

**Conclusion (for your review)**
Across the tools, I found **no published evidence** that SF3A2 itself is targeted by autoantibodies or recognized as an autoantigen in SLE or a related autoimmune disease. Its connection to known SLE antigens is a physical/complex association only. The one autoantibody report in this protein family is against the distinct protein SF3B1 in a cancer context, which does not support SF3A2 status. This makes SF3A2 a **structural/guilt-by-association candidate** rather than a documented autoantigen. (Absence of evidence in these searches is not proof of absence — a targeted immunoprecipitation/proteomics search or an expert review of primary SLE autoantigen screens would be a reasonable next step.)

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: CLNS1A / pICln (P54105) as a potential SLE autoantigen

**What it is (factual):**
- CLNS1A encodes "Methylosome subunit pICln," a 237-aa chaperone that regulates assembly of spliceosomal snRNPs and the methylation of Sm proteins. It forms a 6S pICln–Sm complex with SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPE, SNRPF, SNRPG, and is a component of the 20S methylosome (with PRMT5, WDR77). Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P54105/entry
- So the premise is confirmed: CLNS1A physically associates with Sm core proteins — which are themselves established anti-Sm targets. But CLNS1A acts as a chaperone that *mimics* Sm proteins transiently; it is not a stable member of the mature core snRNP particle that the clinical anti-Sm test captures (UniProt notes the pICln–Sm complex is "unable to assemble into the core snRNP"). Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P54105/entry

**Structure (context only):**
- AlphaFold mean pLDDT 75.5/100 ("Confident"). Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P54105

**Published autoantigen evidence (the key question):**
- A search for CLNS1A/pICln autoantibodies in lupus returned **no papers** directly reporting that CLNS1A/pICln is targeted by autoantibodies in SLE or any related autoimmune disease. Searches returned either off-topic results or an unrelated mechanistic study.
- The one on-topic hit — "CLNS1A regulates genome stability and cell cycle progression to control CD4 T cell function and autoimmunity" (2025) — describes an *intracellular functional role* of CLNS1A in T cells and autoimmunity, **not** CLNS1A being an autoantibody target/autoantigen. Source: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/40540585
- I found no published report of "anti-pICln" or "anti-CLNS1A" autoantibodies in patient sera.

**Human-in-the-loop caveat:** My rules allow complex-level inference only for *established core members* of recognized autoantigen complexes captured by named clinical tests. CLNS1A is a transient chaperone/assembly factor, not a stable Sm-core/snRNP component, so it does not qualify by that criterion. Its association with Sm proteins makes it a plausible structural candidate, but association alone is not autoantigen evidence. You may wish to confirm with a targeted sera/immunoprecipitation literature review, as my tool searches cannot rule out niche reports.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: FUBP1 (Far upstream element-binding protein 1) as an SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity (UniProt)**
- FUBP1 / Far upstream element-binding protein 1, accession Q96AE4, 644 aa. It regulates MYC expression by binding a single-stranded far-upstream element and interacts with PUF60 and JTV1. Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q96AE4/entry
- Note: UniProt describes it as a MYC-regulatory single-stranded DNA/RNA-binding protein. The tools returned **no** data placing FUBP1 inside any of the recognized SLE autoantigen complexes (Sm core, U1 snRNP, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku, Ro/La). Its association with Sm-B/B′, U1-A, U1-C — per your premise — is an interaction, which by itself does not confer autoantigen status.

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold)**
- Mean pLDDT 63.6/100 — "Low" confidence. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q96AE4. (This reflects predicted disorder/flexibility, not autoantigenicity — contextual only.)

**Published autoantigen evidence (Europe PMC)**
- FUBP1 recurs as a **candidate** in the Wang & Roehrl "autoantigen-ome" catalog papers, which profile proteins captured by autoantigen-affinity (DS-affinity) proteomics and link alternative-splicing-related proteins to autoimmune diseases:
  - "A master autoantigen-ome links alternative splicing, female predilection, and COVID-19 to autoimmune diseases" (2022): https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35237749 (preprint: https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR378369)
  - "An Autoantigen-ome from HS-Sultan B-Lymphoblasts…" (2021): https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR307555
- A broader antibody-profiling trial paper also appeared: https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41559617
- My targeted searches for FUBP1 tied to a **named SLE antibody test** or **confirmed SLE patient sera** (anti-FUBP1 in lupus nephritis, Sjögren, scleroderma, etc.) returned only these same catalog/discovery papers — no clinical validation study.

**Interpretation (for your review)**
- The evidence is **catalog/discovery-level**: FUBP1 is flagged as a candidate autoantigen in proteomic screens associated with autoimmunity, but the tools returned no clinical study demonstrating anti-FUBP1 autoantibodies in a defined SLE cohort, and FUBP1 is not part of any established named SLE autoantigen complex or clinical antibody panel. This is more than nothing, but well short of "established."
- Evidence is thin and derives largely from one research group's autoantigen-ome catalogs; independent clinical confirmation would be the sensible next step before any firm claim.

EVIDENCE: EMERGING

## Assessment: Is C1QBP (Q07021) an SLE autoantigen?

**Protein identity (UniProt)**
- C1QBP = Complement component 1 Q subcomponent-binding protein, mitochondrial (gene *C1QBP*, 282 aa). The UniProt record I retrieved lists only microbial-infection-related function/interactions and does **not** document membership in any recognized SLE autoantigen complex (Sm/snRNP, Ro/La, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku). Source: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q07021/entry

**Structural confidence (AlphaFold)**
- Mean pLDDT 75.1 ("Confident"). This speaks only to model reliability, not to autoantigen status. Source: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/Q07021

**Published autoantibody / autoantigen evidence (Europe PMC)**
- I found **no paper that directly demonstrates anti-C1QBP autoantibodies in SLE patients** or validates it with a named clinical antibody test.
- The most relevant hits were broad proteomic **"autoantigen-ome" discovery catalogues** (Wang, Roehrl et al., 2022 — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35237749; preprint https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR378369; related B-lymphoblast autoantigen-ome https://europepmc.org/article/PPR/PPR307555). These surfaced repeatedly for C1QBP-focused queries, suggesting C1QBP may appear as a *candidate* in such screens — **but I cannot confirm from the tool output that C1QBP is explicitly named inside these papers**, and these are unvalidated discovery lists, not disease-specific confirmation.
- Other hits (mitochondria in rheumatic diseases — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36175664; Sjögren's/type I IFN; the 2023 SLE autoantibody update — https://europepmc.org/article/MED/36695053) were topically adjacent but did not, in the returned data, identify C1QBP as an autoantibody target.

**Honest bottom line**
C1QBP is not documented by these tools as an established SLE autoantigen, and no study I retrieved directly shows it is targeted by autoantibodies. There are, at most, broad published autoantigen-screening catalogues that may list it as a candidate — a weak hint rather than established evidence. **Recommended next step for the expert:** check the full text of the Wang/Roehrl autoantigen-ome papers to verify whether C1QBP is explicitly listed, and search for any patient-serum reactivity studies, before drawing conclusions.

EVIDENCE: EMERGING

## Assessment: GIGYF1 (O75420) as a potential SLE autoantigen

**Protein identity & function.** GIGYF1 is the GRB10-interacting GYF protein 1, a 1,035-aa protein that cooperates with GRB10 to regulate tyrosine kinase (IGF1) receptor signaling and also interacts with DDX6. Its documented binding partners are GRB10 and DDX6 — **not** the Sm core/snRNP autoantigen complex. [UniProt: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O75420/entry]

**Structural confidence.** The AlphaFold model is low confidence (mean pLDDT 55.2/100), consistent with a largely disordered protein — a caveat for any structure-based epitope reasoning. [AlphaFold: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/O75420]

**Literature search for autoantigen/autoantibody evidence.** I ran five targeted queries combining GIGYF1 (and its full protein name) with "autoantibody," "autoantigen," "autoimmune disease," "lupus," and SLE terms. None returned any paper reporting GIGYF1 as a target of autoantibodies or as an autoantigen in SLE or a related autoimmune disease. The returned hits were off-topic or concerned genetic susceptibility, not autoantigenicity:
- Autoimmune hepatitis blood transcriptomics [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35312680]
- Shared genetic risk across immune-mediated diseases/schizophrenia [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/31211845]
- Diabetes/Hashimoto's/Sjögren's susceptibility-gene (GWAS/exome) studies [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37528512; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42527560; https://europepmc.org/article/MED/37730603]

These describe gene-level associations at most, which is distinct from a protein being an antibody-targeted autoantigen.

**Interpretation (for your review).** Per the criteria I apply, GIGYF1 is not a documented core component of any recognized SLE autoantigen complex (Sm/snRNP, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku, Ro/La) — its UniProt-listed interactions are with GRB10/DDX6, not the Sm/U1 particle. Any physical association with Sm-B/B', U1-A, or U1-C mentioned in your prompt was not corroborated by the tool data here, and a mere interaction would not by itself confer autoantigen status. I found **no published evidence** that GIGYF1 is itself targeted by autoantibodies.

Suggested next step: if you have a specific interaction dataset (e.g., a proteomics/IP study) linking GIGYF1 to the snRNP, I can search for that primary source directly; otherwise this remains a structural/interaction candidate only.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND

## Assessment: Is COIL (coilin) a published SLE autoantigen?

**What the tools confirm about the protein**
- Coilin (COIL, P38432) is a structural component of nuclear coiled bodies / Cajal bodies, involved in snRNP modification and assembly. Its documented interaction partners are SMN1, AK6, WRAP53/TCAB1, ANKS1B, HMBOX1, PSME3, and UBL5 — note that none of these are the classical SLE autoantigen complexes (Sm core, U1-snRNP, nucleosome, ribosomal P, Ku, Ro/La). [UniProt: https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P38432/entry]
- AlphaFold predicts its structure at low overall confidence (mean pLDDT 58.5/100), consistent with a largely disordered protein — structural modeling here should be treated cautiously. [AlphaFold: https://alphafold.ebi.ac.uk/entry/P38432]

**What the literature searches returned**
I ran six literature queries combining "coilin / p80 / Cajal body" with autoantibody and disease terms (SLE, Sjögren's, nuclear dots, patient sera). The hits were almost entirely:
- General ANA / HEp-2 immunofluorescence-pattern reviews, e.g. the HEp-2 pattern nomenclature consensus [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26347739], ANA fluorescence-pattern reviews [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/42923724], and ANA-as-classification-criteria reviews [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/35128372]; and
- Off-topic coilin cell-biology papers (Cajal body dynamics, aging, spliceosome screens), e.g. [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/11134083] and [https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41562866].

**Important caveat:** these tools returned only titles/authors, not full text. None of the returned records has a title that documents anti-coilin autoantibodies or names coilin as an autoantigen in SLE or a related disease. The ANA-pattern reviews *may* discuss a coilin-associated nuclear-dot pattern internally, but I cannot verify that from the metadata the tool gave me, so I will not claim it.

**Conclusion**
- Coilin only *interacts with / co-localizes near* SLE autoantigens; it is not itself a core subunit of any recognized autoantigen complex, so the "established-by-complex-membership" rule does not apply to it.
- My tool searches did not return any published paper that establishes, or even clearly reports, coilin/p80 as a target of autoantibodies in SLE or related autoimmune disease.

This should be reviewed by an expert: a human familiar with the anti-"nuclear dots"/p80-coilin ANA literature may know of primary reports (e.g., older coiled-body autoantibody work) that my keyword searches did not surface. I'd suggest a targeted full-text/PubMed search on "p80-coilin autoantibody" and screening the full text of the HEp-2 pattern consensus as a next step before finalizing.

EVIDENCE: NONE-FOUND
